findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a database read-modify-write (record.save) inside the User validation pass, making validation side-effectful and non-idempotent. Every failed account-creation attempt (or any other save that triggers email validation) writes to blocked_emails; concurrent requests to the same blocked email race on match_count and can also trigger uniqueness/validation errors whose exceptions propagate out of User.valid? into a 500. Site operators also get match_count incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail feature ships with no writer path anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates the table. The feature is inert in production: nobody can actually block an email without hand-crafting SQL against blocked_emails, so the validation will never fire and the client-side rejectedEmails logic is dead code until a management surface is added.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an interpolated Regexp from the raw SiteSetting value, which raises RegexpError when an admin saves a blacklist/whitelist containing regex metacharacters (e.g. '(', '+', '['). A site admin entering a domain list with an unescaped metacharacter in the settings UI makes every User validation crash with RegexpError, breaking all signup and profile saves until the setting is fixed.

[ADVISORY] The refactor drops email presence/uniqueness validation ordering guarantees by combining into one validates call while keeping the format check gated on email_changed?, so on create (where email_changed? is true only before persistence semantics settle) the if-condition interacts with Rails 3 attribute-change tracking. If email_changed? returns false in any create-path (e.g. legacy import or object built with email then re-assigned same value), no whitelist/blacklist or blocked-email check runs and the user is created unvalidated; the old email_validator had the same if: guard, so this is inherited rather than introduced, but the new blocked-email bypass rides on the same hole.

[ADVISORY] The client trusts server-reported result.values.email and permanently blacklists it in-session, but the server pushes rejectedEmails for any email error including uniqueness, so a user who mistyped an already-registered address then corrects it to that same address in a different case (exact string) is stuck with 'email invalid' until page reload. Signup users who hit a transient email error (e.g. duplicate email they meant to register) get the generic user.email.invalid message on the corrected address within the same session; the form appears broken even though the server would accept it.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (match_count increment + save) inside model validation, so any code path that checks validity without persisting still mutates the blocked_emails row. Every User#valid? call with a changed email that matches a blocked record increments match_count and updates last_match_at — stats become meaningless (a user retyping the email in the signup form over multiple attempts inflates counts, and admin previews/valid? checks in console or background jobs record phantom 'matches'), and the validation path now issues an unconditional UPDATE on every signup attempt.

[ADVISORY] The new spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch (with should_block? stubbed) and never exercises the migrated whitelist/blacklist restriction-setting logic in EmailValidator#validate_each / email_in_restriction_setting?. The email_in_restriction_setting? regex-construction logic (gsub('.', '\.') then interpolated into an unanchored Regexp with alternation) moved from user.rb to email_validator.rb with zero test coverage; a regression in domain matching — e.g., a comma-separated setting producing the wrong alternation, or 'a.com' also matching 'ba.com' because the regex is unanchored — silently breaks signup for whitelisted/blacklisted domains with no failing spec.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Site operators cannot actually block an email except via direct database/rails-console access, so the entire client-side rejectedEmails flow and the new 'user.email.blocked' locale are inert until unrelated future code adds an entry path; the feature is untestable end-to-end in production use as shipped.

[ADVISORY] The new `errors:` and `values:` fields in the failed-create JSON response have no test coverage anywhere in the diff (no users_controller spec touches the create failure payload). The client's rejectedEmails push depends on the exact shape `result.errors.email && result.values`; a rename or reshaping of this payload (e.g., errors keys serialized differently, or values.email normalized to downcase so it never string-matches the typed email in rejectedEmails.contains) silently disables the entire front-end blocking UX with no failing spec to catch it.

[ADVISORY] When a previously rejected email is re-entered, the client shows the generic 'user.email.invalid' message rather than the server's actual blocked-email reason ('user.email.blocked', added in server.en.yml but never surfaced to the user). A user whose email is blocked sees 'is invalid' instead of the more specific 'is not allowed', so they keep retrying variations of a valid-format address that will always be rejected — the new locale string exists but no code path ever displays it to end users, making it dead-on-arrival.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail model and migration ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates blocked_emails, so the feature's stated purpose (blocking emails) is unusable by operators as delivered. Admins deploying this PR gain a blocked_emails table that stays empty forever; blocked-user email validation never fires in production until a separate (unwritten) management path exists, making the entire backend half of this change inert.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at via record.save) inside what the EmailValidator calls during model validation, embedding a DB side effect in the validation path. Every failed user-creation attempt (including validation of other invalid fields on the same record) triggers a blocked_emails UPDATE and commit; concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on save and can raise, and validation no longer being read-only breaks the assumption other call sites (e.g., user.valid? checks in console/jobs) make about being side-effect free.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email check is skipped whenever the whitelist/blacklist check already produced an error (`if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?`), so match statistics are not collected for emails that are both domain-restricted and blocked. Operators using last_match_at/match_count to triage blocked spammers lose all telemetry for any email that also trips the domain restriction, silently undercounting the exact abuse population the feature was built to track.

[ADVISORY] The client rejects an email permanently (rejectedEmails) based on any server-side email error (`result.errors.email`), not specifically the new 'blocked' error, so a transient email error (e.g., uniqueness race on an email the user does not actually own) locks that address out of the form for the session. A user whose email collides with an existing account, or who triggers the domain-restriction message, gets the generic 'user.email.invalid' validation permanently attached to that address even after correcting other fields; they must fully reload to retry, a regression the PR's stated scope (blocked emails only) did not ask for.

[BUG] should_block? increments match_count via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking or atomic UPDATE, so concurrent validations of the same email lose increments. Two signups with the same blocked email validated concurrently both read match_count=5 and both write 6, permanently undercounting; last_match_at also races. Stats drift silently with no way to detect it; fix is UPDATE blocked_emails SET match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = NOW() WHERE email = ?.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? is invoked from inside the User validation pipeline and performs a SELECT plus a save (write) on every invocation, making model validation side-effectful. Any code path that calls valid?/save on a User with a changed email — including password change flows, admin screens, background jobs retrying failed signups — silently writes to blocked_emails, inflating match_count and skewing last_match_at for uses like 'has this email ever been blocked'. A validation method that mutates persistent state couples the check-for-blocked rule to stat collection; the query and the counter increment belong in separate call sites (the counter in the controller/create path).

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup matches exactly (where(email: email)) while nothing in this diff normalizes case on either the stored BlockedEmail.email or the incoming user email, so 'Spam@x.com' does not match a stored 'spam@x.com' row on Postgres. An operator seeds blocked_emails with lowercase addresses (or a user re-registers with mixed case) and the block is silently bypassed — the lookup fails to match what was stored. The compare path and the seed path need one canonical form (e.g. lower(email) on both), otherwise the feature's guarantee ('blocked users can't re-register') is unenforceable by case variation.

[ADVISORY] The new error payload couples the client to ActiveRecord's internal error representation by returning user.errors.to_hash raw, with the client keying on result.errors.email as a bare string discriminator. Any future change to how the User model names its email errors (e.g. moving the blocked check to a :blocked_email attribute, or i18n key renames) silently breaks the client-side rejection cache — the controller still returns 200 with errors keyed differently, the JS guard result.errors.email finds nothing, and the rejectedEmails cache stops populating with no error anywhere. A typed contract (e.g. always emitting an explicit field list or error codes) would make the cross-boundary shape explicit.

[ADVISORY] The email validator (which now includes the BlockedEmail DB query and write) is gated on if: :email_changed?, so the blocked check only runs when the email attribute changed, and an update path that revalidates an unchanged email never consults the blocklist. This is correct for signup but means the blocklist cannot ever affect existing accounts (arguably intended), and more importantly any caller that builds a User and sets email before... the gating means every path that touches email re-triggers the query+write. The coupling of a growing side-effectful lookup to a change-detection gate makes the next change (e.g. 're-check blocked emails on profile update') require restructuring rather than a config flip — worth making the intent explicit (signup-only check in the controller) instead of piggybacking on the attribute-dirty mechanism.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regexp by interpolating the raw whitelist/blacklist SiteSetting content with only '.' escaped, so any other regex metacharacter in the setting ('*', '+', '(', '|', '\') is interpreted as regex syntax or raises. An admin entering a domain list containing e.g. 'foo+bar.com' or an unbalanced '(' gets RegexpError raised inside user validation — the signup endpoint's rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid does not cover it, so account creation 500s site-wide until the setting is reverted. This is inherited from the deleted User code, but this diff moves it into a shared validator now applied to every email-validating model, widening the blast radius; a split-on-pipe + escaped alternation would remove the parse risk.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email check mutates the database inside model validation: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves on every validation run. Every failed User#save (including repeated retries of the same signup, admin edits, and any code path that calls valid?) bumps match_count and last_match_at, so the stats that the PR's own spec says exist to show 'whether those emails have ever been blocked' are inflated by pure validation noise and no longer mean a real block attempt; stats consumers (admins loading the table) get wrong data.

[ADVISORY] The client displays the generic 'user.email.invalid' message for any email the server rejected, discarding the server's actual error reason, and the new server locale 'user.email.blocked' never reaches the user. A user with a well-formed email that was rejected by domain whitelist/blacklist or BlockedEmail sees 'invalid' — a factually wrong message that the original server intent (distinct not_allowed vs blocked messages, preserved in server.en.yml:731-733) was specifically designed to distinguish; support burden from confused users who retry the same address.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, seed, or rake task inserts or updates rows (only test fabricators do). Operators cannot actually use the feature this PR claims to deliver; the only production writes are the match_count side-effects from should_block?, so the table stays empty and 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' silently does nothing until unrelated code is written later.

[ADVISORY] The failed-create response now echoes raw user attributes (name, username, email) back to the client via the new `values` payload. The account-creation error path (reachable by any anonymous visitor hitting POST /users) now leaks server-held user attributes it did not previously return; combined with email uniqueness validation this lets an anonymous caller probe which name/username/email combinations the server considers taken — an enumeration surface added solely to populate a client cache, not required by the original intent of showing blocked-email feedback.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the raw email string with no case normalization, so `WHERE email = 'block@spamfromhome.org'` misses `Block@SpamFromHome.org`, `BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, etc. A user whose address was blocked (or a banned spammer re-registering) bypasses the entire blocklist simply by varying the case of the local part or domain during signup — the blocklist becomes trivially defeatable, which is the feature's only security purpose.

[BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an unanchored regex `@(#{domains})` matching anywhere in the string, so a blacklisted domain `spam.com` also matches `user@spam.com.attacker.org` and `user@spam.com.evil.tld`. A user on a blacklisted provider registers with an address whose real domain is `spam.com.attacker.org` and passes the blacklist; conversely a whitelist-only site rejects legitimate addresses containing a whitelisted domain as a suffix. This defect existed in the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting? and is carried unchanged into the new validator.

[ADVISORY] The site-setting string is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped (gsub('.', '\.')), so any other regex metacharacter in the setting (an unbalanced `(`, `*`, `+`) raises RegexpError. An admin pasting a domain list containing `*` or unbalanced parens into email_domains_blacklist/whitelist makes every signup and every email update raise RegexpError, returning a 500 on the public account-creation endpoint until the setting is reverted; the interpolating line is new in this diff.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a write (match_count += 1, save) inside model validation on the public, unauthenticated account-creation path. An unauthenticated attacker hammering POST /users triggers a read-modify-write on blocked_emails for every attempt, letting them inflate match_count/last_match_at (destroying the operator's blocklist statistics) and generating DB write load proportional to request rate with no rate limit in this path.

[ADVISORY] Email validation via the new `email: true, if: :email_changed?` guard is skipped whenever the email is unchanged, but BlockedEmail rows can be added after an account exists, so a previously-valid email is never re-checked against the blocklist on subsequent saves. Operators who load the blocklist after spam signups already occurred cannot lock those existing accounts out through this mechanism; the same drift applies to whitelist/blacklist changes, matching the old behavior but now the only enforcement point.

[ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? in both cases, so the validator test verifies the mock's return value, not the validator's real interaction with BlockedEmail, and the whitelist/blacklist restriction branches in lib/validators/email_validator.rb (lines 5-13) have zero coverage in this spec. I checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb (the only test files in the diff referencing these symbols). No spec ever runs EmailValidator against a real BlockedEmail row or with SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist set. A regression in the moved whitelist/blacklist logic (e.g. inverted regexp escape or wrong setting precedence, which was hand-copied from the deleted User#email_validator with no existing user_spec updated) passes green, and admins who rely on email_domains_blacklist find it silently stops blocking after this refactor ships.

[ADVISORY] The 'doesn't add an error' test stubs should_block? to return false and then asserts record.errors[:email] is blank, which is also exactly the outcome when the entire BlockedEmail call is removed from EmailValidator — the test cannot distinguish correct code from code that never checks the blocklist. A future refactor that drops the BlockedEmail.should_block? call from validate_each (or wraps it in a condition that never fires) still passes this spec, because the only assertion is absence of errors and the only code under test beyond the stub is the skipped if-guard. The strongest rebuttal — 'the companion test at line 17 covers the true case' — doesn't survive, because both cases stub the same seam, so neither exercises the guard's actual dispatch to the real method; a maintainer changing the guard condition (e.g. inverting record.errors[attribute].blank?) gets a passing suite while blocked users register.

[ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it — and no backfill from the existing email_domains_blacklist site setting, so the feature is inert for every existing install. Operators upgrading with this migration get an empty blocked_emails table and no path to insert rows; blocked-email enforcement silently blocks nothing until unrelated future work adds a writer. Existing blacklist settings still work via EmailValidator, but the new mechanism the diff promises is unusable.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (record.save incrementing match_count and last_match_at) inside a validation path, so every account-creation or user-save attempt that reaches the email validator issues a read-modify-write against blocked_emails. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email race on match_count (lost updates), and a failed/rolled-back outer transaction discards the statistics; under signup spam the blocked_emails row becomes a write hotspot on every validation run, including validations that ultimately don't persist the user.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup uses case-sensitive WHERE email = ? on a Postgres string column, so an address stored as 'bad@spam.org' does not match 'Bad@spam.org' and the block is bypassed. Anyone whose email was blocked (once a writer exists, e.g. seeded via rake) bypasses the block by varying letter case, since users can register with a mixed-case address that never matches the stored row.

[ADVISORY] The email format/blocked validation is gated on if: :email_changed?, so existing users whose stored (invalid) email is unchanged never re-validated, but any user update that touches the email column re-runs the whole EmailValidator including the blocked-list write in should_block?. Users whose email was accepted under the old rules (e.g. domain not previously blacklisted, then blacklisted) keep working until they change email — acceptable — but every email edit now incurs the blocked_emails read/write side effect even in contexts like admin user edits where a silent match_count increment on a block-listed address is surprising.

[ADVISORY] should_block? increments and saves match statistics with a bare `record.save` whose failure is silently swallowed, and the blocking decision returns regardless of whether the stats write succeeded. If the save fails (unique-index race on concurrent validations, or any validation failure on the BlockedEmail row), match_count/last_match_at are silently lost while the block decision still returns — operators inspecting last_match_at to see which blocked emails are actively being attempted get an undercount with no error logged anywhere.

[ADVISORY] EmailValidator performs a persistent write (BlockedEmail.should_block? → save) as a side effect of model validation, so match_count is incremented every time validation runs, not once per actual signup attempt. Any code path that validates a User multiple times before saving (double submit from the client, `valid?` checks followed by `save`, admin screens calling valid?) inflates match_count and advances last_match_at multiple times per attempt, corrupting the statistics the feature exists to collect; the write also commits even when the surrounding user save later fails, so a failed signup still counts.

[ADVISORY] The values.email echoed back to the client comes from user.attributes, which is the model's stored (normalized) email, not the string the user typed, so the client-side rejectedEmails check compares a normalized address against the raw input and never matches when the two differ. When the server normalizes email case (e.g. downcasing before validation), the client pushes the normalized value into rejectedEmails while the user's typed email still differs; the new client-side 'invalid' rejection never fires, the user retries the same address, and gets the server round-trip and generic failure each time — the feature degrades to its pre-diff behavior with no error surfaced.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Yes. The candidate flags that the blocked-email check method mutates state (increments match_count/last_match_at and saves) even when merely validating/checking, i.e., a read-like operation causing side effects and misleading semantics. This aligns with the golden concern about should_block_email? having side effects and potential concurrency/statistical correctness problems.

per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: [BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an unanchored regex `@(#{domains})` matching anywhere in the string, so a blacklisted domain `spam.com` also matches `user@spam.com.attacker.org` and `user@spam.com.evil.tld`. A user on a blacklisted provider registers with an address whose real domain is `spam.com.attacker.org` and passes the blacklist; conversely a whitelist-only site rejects legitimate addresses containing a whitelisted domain as a suffix. This defect existed in the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting? and is carried unchanged into the new validator.
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Yes. Both point to the same core bug: the regex `@(#{domains})` is not properly anchored to the end/boundary of the domain, so it can match a whitelisted/blacklisted domain as a substring within a longer domain (e.g., `evil.example.com` or `spam.com.attacker.org`), enabling restriction bypass or incorrect matches.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both the golden and candidate describe the same vulnerability: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a case-sensitive email lookup without normalization, allowing blocked addresses to bypass the blocklist by changing letter casing (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com).

The feature is inert in production: nobody can actually block an email without hand-crafting SQL against blocked_emails, so the validation will never fire and the client-side rejectedEmails logic is dead code until a management surface is added.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and wires it into `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), plus client-side caching of rejected emails. However, within this diff there is no admin UI, controller/API, rake task, seed, or any other code path to create/manage `blocked_emails` records—only read/update via `should_block?`. So the review concern that the feature has no management surface in the PR is grounded in what’s shown, even if records could still be inserted manually outside the app.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an interpolated Regexp from the raw SiteSetting value, which raises RegexpError when an admin saves a blacklist/whitelist containing regex metacharacters (e.g. '(', '+', '['). A site admin entering a domain list with an unescaped metacharacter in the settings UI makes every User validation crash with RegexpError, breaking all signup and profile saves until the setting is fixed.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) from the raw SiteSetting value after only escaping dots via setting.gsub('.', '\\.'). Other regex metacharacters in the admin-provided whitelist/blacklist (e.g. '(', '+', '[') are not escaped, so an invalid pattern can raise RegexpError during validation, breaking user saves/signups while the setting remains malformed. This behavior is directly present in the diff (and mirrors the removed implementation).

If email_changed? returns false in any create-path (e.g. legacy import or object built with email then re-assigned same value), no whitelist/blacklist or blocked-email check runs and the user is created unvalidated; the old email_validator had the same if: guard, so this is inherited rather than introduced, but the new blocked-email bypass rides on the same hole.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly gates the new EmailValidator (which now contains the blocked-email check via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) behind `if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). That means any code path where Rails reports `email_changed?` as false will skip whitelist/blacklist and the newly added blocked-email enforcement. Whether such a create-path exists depends on Rails 3 change-tracking semantics and caller behavior, which is not provable from the diff alone, so this is an edge-case concern rather than a clearly verifiable defect. The “presence/uniqueness ordering guarantees” part isn’t concretely demonstrated by the diff, but the conditional validator gating is diff-grounded and actionable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client trusts server-reported result.values.email and permanently blacklists it in-session, but the server pushes rejectedEmails for any email error including uniqueness, so a user who mistyped an already-registered address then corrects it to that same address in a different case (exact string) is stuck with 'email invalid' until page reload. Signup users who hit a transient email error (e.g. duplicate email they meant to register) get the generic user.email.invalid message on the corrected address within the same session; the form appears broken even though the server would accept it.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed signup response with `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails`, and subsequent client-side validation immediately fails for that exact string with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (see `contains(email)` branch). Because the server now always returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: ... slice('email')` on any create failure, this caching applies to *all* email errors (including uniqueness), and it also discards the server’s specific email error (e.g. `user.email.blocked`) on subsequent attempts in the same session. However, the finding’s claim that changing case would still be blocked isn’t directly supported by the diff, since `contains` is an exact string match.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (match_count increment + save) inside model validation, so any code path that checks validity without persisting still mutates the blocked_emails row. Every User#valid? call with a changed email that matches a blocked record increments match_count and updates last_match_at — stats become meaningless (a user retyping the email in the signup form over multiple attempts inflates counts, and admin previews/valid? checks in console or background jobs record phantom 'matches'), and the validation path now issues an unconditional UPDATE on every signup attempt.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator` which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a write whenever a matching blocked_emails row exists: it increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s. That means any `User#valid?` / validation pass (even without persisting the User) will mutate `blocked_emails`, inflating stats and issuing an UPDATE on each validation attempt. This behavior is directly verifiable from the added code paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch (with should_block? stubbed) and never exercises the migrated whitelist/blacklist restriction-setting logic in EmailValidator#validate_each / email_in_restriction_setting?. The email_in_restriction_setting? regex-construction logic (gsub('.', '\.') then interpolated into an unanchored Regexp with alternation) moved from user.rb to email_validator.rb with zero test coverage; a regression in domain matching — e.g., a comma-separated setting producing the wrong alternation, or 'a.com' also matching 'ba.com' because the regex is unanchored — silently breaks signup for whitelisted/blacklisted domains with no failing spec.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the domain whitelist/blacklist checking logic from `User#email_validator` / `email_in_restriction_setting?` into the new `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`), but the added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only exercises the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch (and stubs it). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new `errors:` and `values:` fields in the failed-create JSON response have no test coverage anywhere in the diff (no users_controller spec touches the create failure payload). adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the `UsersController#create` failure JSON, and the client now relies on that exact payload shape (`result.errors.email && result.values` then `pushObject(result.values.email)`) to populate `rejectedEmails`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When a previously rejected email is re-entered, the client shows the generic 'user.email.invalid' message rather than the server's actual blocked-email reason ('user.email.blocked', added in server.en.yml but never surfaced to the user). A user whose email is blocked sees 'is invalid' instead of the more specific 'is not allowed', so they keep retrying variations of a valid-format address that will always be rejected — the new locale string exists but no code path ever displays it to end users, making it dead-on-arrival.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, once an email submission fails, the email is added to `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Subsequent client-side validation short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and always returns `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the server-side reason (e.g., `user.email.blocked` added in `server.en.yml` and used by the new `EmailValidator`). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail model and migration ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates blocked_emails, so the feature's stated purpose (blocking emails) is unusable by operators as delivered. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and wires it into `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but nowhere in the shown changes is there any code path (controller/admin UI/seed/task) that creates or manages `blocked_emails` rows. As delivered in this diff alone, the table will remain empty unless populated out-of-band, so the new blocking capability is effectively inert for operators without an added management mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at via record.save) inside what the EmailValidator calls during model validation, embedding a DB side effect in the validation path. Every failed user-creation attempt (including validation of other invalid fields on the same record) triggers a blocked_emails UPDATE and commit; concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on save and can raise, and validation no longer being read-only breaks the assumption other call sites (e.g., user.valid? checks in console/jobs) make about being side-effect free.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, and it is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` during model validation (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`). This makes `user.valid?`/validation paths have DB side effects (updating `blocked_emails`) even when the overall record is invalid for other reasons, which is an architectural/behavioral concern introduced by the change. The specific concurrency/race/raise claims are speculative, but the side-effect-in-validation is directly grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email check is skipped whenever the whitelist/blacklist check already produced an error (`if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?`), so match statistics are not collected for emails that are both domain-restricted and blocked. Operators using last_match_at/match_count to triage blocked spammers lose all telemetry for any email that also trips the domain restriction, silently undercounting the exact abuse population the feature was built to track.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email path is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since the whitelist/blacklist checks above can add an error to `record.errors[attribute]`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` will not be called in those cases. But `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is also responsible for incrementing `match_count` and setting `last_match_at` when a record exists, so those statistics will not be updated for emails that trigger both a domain restriction error and exist in `blocked_emails`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client rejects an email permanently (rejectedEmails) based on any server-side email error (`result.errors.email`), not specifically the new 'blocked' error, so a transient email error (e.g., uniqueness race on an email the user does not actually own) locks that address out of the form for the session. A user whose email collides with an existing account, or who triggers the domain-restriction message, gets the generic 'user.email.invalid' validation permanently attached to that address even after correcting other fields; they must fully reload to retry, a regression the PR's stated scope (blocked emails only) did not ask for.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any server response containing `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (no check for the specific new `user.email.blocked` case). The email validator then hard-fails locally for that exact email via `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, preventing any further attempts with that email for the session without reload. This behavior is directly introduced by the diff and can incorrectly “lock out” retrying the same email after transient/conditional email errors (e.g., race/temporary uniqueness failure) and also collapses distinct server-side email errors (blocked/not_allowed/etc.) into a generic invalid message.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? increments match_count via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking or atomic UPDATE, so concurrent validations of the same email lose increments. Two signups with the same blocked email validated concurrently both read match_count=5 and both write 6, permanently undercounting; last_match_at also races. Stats drift silently with no way to detect it; fix is UPDATE blocked_emails SET match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = NOW() WHERE email = ?.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new file `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), the counter and timestamp are updated via a non-atomic read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`. With concurrent validations for the same blocked email, two processes can both read the same `match_count` and overwrite each other’s increment, and `last_match_at` can race as well. The diff shows no locking (`lock!`) or atomic SQL update to prevent lost updates, so the described undercounting/drift is a real correctness issue in the introduced code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? is invoked from inside the User validation pipeline and performs a SELECT plus a save (write) on every invocation, making model validation side-effectful. Any code path that calls valid?/save on a User with a changed email — including password change flows, admin screens, background jobs retrying failed signups — silently writes to blocked_emails, inflating match_count and skewing last_match_at for uses like 'has this email ever been blocked'. A validation method that mutates persistent state couples the check-for-blocked rule to stat collection; the query and the counter increment belong in separate call sites (the counter in the controller/create path).

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `User` now runs `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` and the new `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when there are no prior email errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a SELECT and, if a record exists, mutates persistent state (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = Time.zone.now`, `record.save`). This makes validation side-effectful and causes writes on any validation of a user with a changed email, which can inflate `match_count`/skew `last_match_at` beyond just the signup/create path. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded architectural concern, though not necessarily an immediate functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup matches exactly (where(email: email)) while nothing in this diff normalizes case on either the stored BlockedEmail.email or the incoming user email, so 'Spam@x.com' does not match a stored 'spam@x.com' row on Postgres. An operator seeds blocked_emails with lowercase addresses (or a user re-registers with mixed case) and the block is silently bypassed — the lookup fails to match what was stored. The compare path and the seed path need one canonical form (e.g. lower(email) on both), otherwise the feature's guarantee ('blocked users can't re-register') is unenforceable by case variation.

[ADVISORY] The new error payload couples the client to ActiveRecord's internal error representation by returning user.errors.to_hash raw, with the client keying on result.errors.email as a bare string discriminator. Any future change to how the User model names its email errors (e.g. moving the blocked check to a :blocked_email attribute, or i18n key renames) silently breaks the client-side rejection cache — the controller still returns 200 with errors keyed differently, the JS guard result.errors.email finds nothing, and the rejectedEmails cache stops populating with no error anywhere. A typed contract (e.g. always emitting an explicit field list or error codes) would make the cross-boundary shape explicit.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows the server now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` (users_controller.rb), and the client logic depends on that exact shape: `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }` (create_account_controller.js). This does couple the client to the server’s per-attribute error keys (e.g., the presence of an `email` key) and provides no explicit/typed contract (codes/fields) beyond ActiveModel’s hash structure. If the server were to report the email-related failure under a different attribute key, this cache population would stop without an explicit failure in this JS path. It’s a cross-boundary design/robustness concern grounded in the diff, not a currently verifiable runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email validator (which now includes the BlockedEmail DB query and write) is gated on if: :email_changed?, so the blocked check only runs when the email attribute changed, and an update path that revalidates an unchanged email never consults the blocklist. This is correct for signup but means the blocklist cannot ever affect existing accounts (arguably intended), and more importantly any caller that builds a User and sets email before... the gating means every path that touches email re-triggers the query+write. The coupling of a growing side-effectful lookup to a change-detection gate makes the next change (e.g. 're-check blocked emails on profile update') require restructuring rather than a config flip — worth making the intent explicit (signup-only check in the controller) instead of piggybacking on the attribute-dirty mechanism.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb`, the new validator is `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`) performs `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which does a DB lookup plus increments `match_count`/updates `last_match_at` and `save`s. This means the blocklist check (and its side effects) only runs when Rails considers `email_changed?` true, so validations on an unchanged email won’t consult the blocklist, while any path that triggers `email_changed?` will re-run the query+write during validation. That’s an architectural/intent clarity concern grounded in the diff, not a clearly verifiable functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regexp by interpolating the raw whitelist/blacklist SiteSetting content with only '.' escaped, so any other regex metacharacter in the setting ('*', '+', '(', '|', '\') is interpreted as regex syntax or raises. An admin entering a domain list containing e.g. 'foo+bar.com' or an unbalanced '(' gets RegexpError raised inside user validation — the signup endpoint's rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid does not cover it, so account creation 500s site-wide until the setting is reverted. This is inherited from the deleted User code, but this diff moves it into a shared validator now applied to every email-validating model, widening the blast radius; a split-on-pipe + escaped alternation would remove the parse risk.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp via `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains = setting.gsub('.', '\.')` only escapes dots. Any other regex metacharacters in the SiteSetting string (e.g. `+`, `*`, `(`, `|`, `\`) will be interpreted as regex syntax and can change matching semantics or raise RegexpError. This validator runs during model validation (`validates :email, email: true` in app/models/user.rb), and the signup controller rescue shown only handles ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid, so a RegexpError would bubble up and likely 500 account creation until the setting is fixed. The diff moves this logic into a shared validator class, so the problematic behavior remains and becomes easier to apply broadly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email check mutates the database inside model validation: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves on every validation run. Every failed User#save (including repeated retries of the same signup, admin edits, and any code path that calls valid?) bumps match_count and last_match_at, so the stats that the PR's own spec says exist to show 'whether those emails have ever been blocked' are inflated by pure validation noise and no longer mean a real block attempt; stats consumers (admins loading the table) get wrong data.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. The candidate flags that the blocked-email check method mutates state (increments match_count/last_match_at and saves) even when merely validating/checking, i.e., a read-like operation causing side effects and misleading semantics. This aligns with the golden concern about should_block_email? having side effects and potential concurrency/statistical correctness problems.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client displays the generic 'user.email.invalid' message for any email the server rejected, discarding the server's actual error reason, and the new server locale 'user.email.blocked' never reaches the user. A user with a well-formed email that was rejected by domain whitelist/blacklist or BlockedEmail sees 'invalid' — a factually wrong message that the original server intent (distinct not_allowed vs blocked messages, preserved in server.en.yml:731-733) was specifically designed to distinguish; support burden from confused users who retry the same address.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any server-side rejection that includes `result.errors.email` causes the submitted email to be added to `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Subsequent validation short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a failed `InputValidation` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the actual server error (e.g., `user.email.not_allowed` from whitelist/blacklist or the new `user.email.blocked` from `EmailValidator`). This makes the client show a factually wrong inline/field error message for blocked/forbidden emails, and the new `user.email.blocked` reason is not used in the client-side validation UI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, seed, or rake task inserts or updates rows (only test fabricators do). Operators cannot actually use the feature this PR claims to deliver; the only production writes are the match_count side-effects from should_block?, so the table stays empty and 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' silently does nothing until unrelated code is written later.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `blocked_emails` (migration) and `BlockedEmail` with `should_block?` that only reads a matching row and updates `match_count/last_match_at` (a side-effect write). The new `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but there is no production code in the diff that creates or manages `BlockedEmail` rows (no controller/admin UI/seed/rake task), only test fabricators. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The failed-create response now echoes raw user attributes (name, username, email) back to the client via the new `values` payload. The account-creation error path (reachable by any anonymous visitor hitting POST /users) now leaks server-held user attributes it did not previously return; combined with email uniqueness validation this lets an anonymous caller probe which name/username/email combinations the server considers taken — an enumeration surface added solely to populate a client cache, not required by the original intent of showing blocked-email feedback.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the new `values` payload is `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, which (in the failed create path) will reflect the just-submitted attributes, not “server-held” attributes about existing users. It does not expose other users’ names/emails. Also, uniqueness/enumeration via error feedback already existed because the response already included `user.errors.full_messages` inside `message`; adding `values` does not newly enable probing which emails/usernames are taken (though it may make client UX easier).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the raw email string with no case normalization, so `WHERE email = 'block@spamfromhome.org'` misses `Block@SpamFromHome.org`, `BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, etc. A user whose address was blocked (or a banned spammer re-registering) bypasses the entire blocklist simply by varying the case of the local part or domain during signup — the blocklist becomes trivially defeatable, which is the feature's only security purpose.
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden and candidate describe the same vulnerability: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a case-sensitive email lookup without normalization, allowing blocked addresses to bypass the blocklist by changing letter casing (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an unanchored regex `@(#{domains})` matching anywhere in the string, so a blacklisted domain `spam.com` also matches `user@spam.com.attacker.org` and `user@spam.com.evil.tld`. A user on a blacklisted provider registers with an address whose real domain is `spam.com.attacker.org` and passes the blacklist; conversely a whitelist-only site rejects legitimate addresses containing a whitelisted domain as a suffix. This defect existed in the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting? and is carried unchanged into the new validator.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both point to the same core bug: the regex `@(#{domains})` is not properly anchored to the end/boundary of the domain, so it can match a whitelisted/blacklisted domain as a substring within a longer domain (e.g., `evil.example.com` or `spam.com.attacker.org`), enabling restriction bypass or incorrect matches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The site-setting string is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped (gsub('.', '\.')), so any other regex metacharacter in the setting (an unbalanced `(`, `*`, `+`) raises RegexpError. An admin pasting a domain list containing `*` or unbalanced parens into email_domains_blacklist/whitelist makes every signup and every email update raise RegexpError, returning a 500 on the public account-creation endpoint until the setting is reverted; the interpolating line is new in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` comes from the site setting with only `.` escaped (`setting.gsub('.', '\\.')`). If the setting string contains other regex metacharacters (e.g., `(`, `*`, `+`, unbalanced parens), `Regexp.new` can raise `RegexpError`, and there’s no rescue here, so user creation/email validation could 500. Note: the diff also shows essentially the same regex-building code was present before in `User#email_in_restriction_setting?` and got moved, so the finding’s claim that the interpolating line is entirely new is not accurate, but the crashable behavior is present in the post-diff code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a write (match_count += 1, save) inside model validation on the public, unauthenticated account-creation path. An unauthenticated attacker hammering POST /users triggers a read-modify-write on blocked_emails for every attempt, letting them inflate match_count/last_match_at (destroying the operator's blocklist statistics) and generating DB write load proportional to request rate with no rate limit in this path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` into `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` does a read-modify-write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) whenever a blocked email record exists (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Thus unauthenticated repeated signup attempts with a blocked email will generate DB writes and can inflate the blocklist statistics, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Email validation via the new `email: true, if: :email_changed?` guard is skipped whenever the email is unchanged, but BlockedEmail rows can be added after an account exists, so a previously-valid email is never re-checked against the blocklist on subsequent saves. Operators who load the blocklist after spam signups already occurred cannot lock those existing accounts out through this mechanism; the same drift applies to whitelist/blacklist changes, matching the old behavior but now the only enforcement point.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb`, the new validator hook is `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator` is where the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` check lives. That means blocked-email enforcement (and domain whitelist/blacklist enforcement) only runs when the email attribute changes; saving an existing user without changing email will not re-check against newly-added `BlockedEmail` rows. The finding’s core claim is therefore grounded in the diff, though whether this is a “bug” depends on intended scope (the prior domain restriction logic already had the same `if: :email_changed?` behavior).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? in both cases, so the validator test verifies the mock's return value, not the validator's real interaction with BlockedEmail, and the whitelist/blacklist restriction branches in lib/validators/email_validator.rb (lines 5-13) have zero coverage in this spec. adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? to true/false, so the test only asserts that EmailValidator adds/no-adds an error given the stubbed return value, not that it correctly integrates with the real BlockedEmail model behavior. Also, the whitelist/blacklist branches added in lib/validators/email_validator.rb (the SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist checks) are never exercised in this spec (no SiteSetting setup), and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb only tests BlockedEmail.should_block? directly. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 'doesn't add an error' test stubs should_block? to return false and then asserts record.errors[:email] is blank, which is also exactly the outcome when the entire BlockedEmail call is removed from EmailValidator — the test cannot distinguish correct code from code that never checks the blocklist. If `EmailValidator#validate_each` removed (or never executed) the `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` call, no blocked error would be added for `bad@spamclub.com` (absent whitelist/blacklist settings in the spec), so that example would fail. Any code path that validates a User multiple times before saving (double submit from the client, `valid?` checks followed by `save`, admin screens calling valid?) inflates match_count and advances last_match_at multiple times per attempt, corrupting the statistics the feature exists to collect; the write also commits even when the surrounding user save later fails, so a failed signup still counts.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when there are no other email errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) mutates and persists state by incrementing `match_count`, setting `last_match_at`, and calling `record.save`.
